units.text: 1. Diet quality and the presence and abundance of conspecifics feeding on the same food resource are critical factors that affect functional traits of many animal species and influence ecological processes. 2. We hypothesized that in insects whose larvae live in groups of varying sizes in ephemeral and nutritionally variable environments, extreme macronutrient content in the feeding substrate is a barrier for optimal performance that can be overcome by the collective feeding behaviour of large numbers of larvae. 3. We experimentally examined how multiple immature and adult traits of the polyphagous tephritid fruit fly, Anastrepha ludens, vary as a function of the quality of its larval diet (protein + carbohydrate [P + C] content of 8.0%–12.6% w/w, and protein-to-carbohydrate [P/C] ratio of 1.8–0.11) across extreme levels of conspecific larval densities (60–600 larvae/60 g of diet). 4. Overall, we found positive effects on survival of immature and adult stages, the duration of the larval stage, pupal weight and adult emergence of flies, as dietary P + C content increased, followed by negative effects when the diet had extremely high carbohydrate-biased macronutrient content. Larval density had positive, negative and curvilinear effects depending on the macronutrient composition of the food, resulting in a range of fly responses through a continuous scale of macronutrient content and larval density combinations. Optimal performance of A. ludens, in terms of larval development time, body weight and survival to adulthood, was found when the diet consisted of low P + C content and high P/C ratios, and low larval densities. 5. Our findings point to a diet-mediated relationship between density and survival to the adult stage, suggesting that large numbers (up to a point) of larvae can balance negative effects of conspecific competition when food is characterised by high macronutrient content and low P/C ratios. We conclude that diet quality and conspecific density interact in complex ways to shape trait expression and performance in a frugivorous fly. Addressing this interaction is key to advance the understanding of the mechanisms behind changes in population dynamics in insect species living in groups confined in isolated and ephemeral resources.

The Mexican fruit fly, Anastrepha ludens (Loew), is a polyphagous species distributed from southern Texas to Costa Rica, where it can exploit the fruit of c. 38 wild and cultivated plant species within 11 families (Birke & Aluja, 2018; Birke et al., 2013; Norrbom, 2004). It is a potentially invasive fly species that is currently expanding its geographical range in Mexico to exploit novel hosts (M. Aluja, personal observation; Aluja et al., 2014; Birke et al., 2013). There are, however, limits to its polyphagy (Birke et al., 2015), and it is suggested that phytochemical and nutritional characteristics of fruit, or the lack of an adequate gut microbiota, could restrict the ability of this fly species to exploit novel hosts (Aluja et al., 2014, 2021; Birke et al., 2015; Pascacio-Villafán et al., 2016). Anastrepha ludens females lay eggs in clutches (1–45 eggs per clutch) and tend to oviposit in mature-green fruit with relatively low nutritional content (Aluja et al., 2019). One assumed strategy used by A. ludens females to overcome adverse phytochemical/nutritional conditions in the host fruit for their offspring is to increase the number of eggs oviposited so that many larvae can generate metabolic heat leading to the growth of beneficial micro-organisms for the larvae (Díaz-Fleischer & Aluja, 2003). Larval density levels of A. ludens in the field vary widely among host plants (Aluja et al., 2000a, 2000b). For instance, in Casimiroa greggii (S. Watson) F. Chiang (Rutaceae), a wild host with small fruit (c. 2 cm in diameter), little pulp and large seeds occupying c. 85% of the whole fruit, A. ludens larvae feed on the seeds and the number of larvae per fruit ranges from one to three (Emilio Acosta, pers. comm.; Aluja et al., 2000a; Plummer et al., 1941). In the case of much larger cultivated hosts such as grapefruit (Citrus paradisi L. [Rutaceae]), a single fruit can harbour between six and more than 80 larvae (depending on the cultivar) (Emilio Acosta, pers. comm.; Aluja et al., 2000a, 2000b). Extreme larval infestations have been reported in grapefruit infested in the laboratory and then transferred to the field for larval development, with a range of one to 201 larvae per fruit (Thomas, 1997).

Here, we hypothesized that extreme macronutrient content in the larval feeding substrate of frugivorous insects is a barrier for optimal performance that can be overcome by the collective feeding behaviour of large numbers of larvae. To test this hypothesis, we experimentally examined how multiple traits of A. ludens were expressed across extreme levels of dietary macronutrient content (protein plus carbohydrate combinations) and across extreme levels of conspecific larval densities in the larval feeding substrate. We predicted (a) curvilinear (concave-down or concave-up) responses of A. ludens traits as a function of the macronutrient content of diet at low larval density treatments, and negative responses with increasing macronutrient content at extremely high larval densities; and (b) concave-down responses of A. ludens traits with increasing larval density in diets with extremely high macronutrient content but not in balanced ones. We adopted a modelling trait approach to further understand the interactions in larval environments that regulate the performance of tephritid flies.

Anastrepha ludens were obtained from a laboratory colony maintained as described in Aluja et al. (2009). The last introduction of wild flies stemming from citrus fruit to this colony was made 2.5 years before the beginning of the experiments reported here. Adult flies were kept in 60 cm long × 30 cm tall × 30 cm wide Plexiglass cages at a density of 0.414 flies per cm 2 and provided ad libitum access to food (3:1 mixture of sugar:hydrolysed protein) and water. Females oviposited in artificial devices filled with transparent silicon (Aluja et al., 2009). Eggs were washed with tap water through a plastic strainer to remove all the silicon, then washed with a 2% (w/v) sodium benzoate solution and finally rinsed again with tap water. We worked with a laboratory-reared insect pest species that does not require ethical approval for animal use. We are aware of animal well-being's importance and followed the principles of the 3 Rs (replacement, reduction and refinement) applied to scientific procedures when animals included in international regulations are used (Russell & Burch, 1959).

The experiment was designed with the Design-Expert® 10 Software (Anderson & Whitcomb, 2005). The predictor variables were the macronutrient content of diets (percentage of protein plus carbohydrate) and larval density (larvae per 60 g of diet) (Figure 1). We constructed a geometric experimental design space constrained by carbohydrate:protein percentages in the range of 2.84:5.12–11.35:1.28 and total macronutrient content of 8.0%–12.6%, and by conspecific larval densities in the range of 60–600 larvae per 60 g of diet (Figure 1). The experiment consisted of 25 diet (with varying macronutrient content and nutrient ratios, see Table S1) × larval density combinations distributed equidistantly across the whole design space, each replicated five times for a total of 125 randomized experimental runs conducted in one block (Figure 1). An experimental run consisted in an individual Petri dish with 60 g of diet and larvae

from which response variables were measured. The following traits of A. ludens were considered as response variables: (a) the number of pupating individuals, (b) the proportion of survival from larva to pupa, (c) the duration of the larval stage (days), (d) pupal weight (mg), (e) the proportion of adult emergence and (f) the proportion of survival from larva to adult. These traits are related to fitness in frugivorous tephritids and are all sensitive to environmental conditions (Birke & Aluja, 2018; Hafsi et al., 2016; Jácome et al., 1999; Wu et al., 2011). Details on how these traits were measured are given in Section 2.5.

Trait | Trait type | Functionality
Larval development time | Life history | Development time is used to describe fitness (Brückner et al., 2018). Individuals in a population can improve their fitness if they develop faster and have additional time to find mates and reproduce (Metcalfe & Monaghan, 2003). Conversely, longer larval development times result in a greater exposure to natural enemies/predators and a higher risk of pathogen infection, with a resulting increased mortality (Aluja et al., 2005; Benrey & Denno, 1997; Rostas & Hilker, 2003). Shorter larval development times in tephritids improve intra- and inter-competition abilities and facilitate establishment of invasive species (Duyck et al., 2008). As demonstrated in Aluja et al. (2014), larval developmental time is directly linked to the quality of the food ingested by the larvae (host plant). A feeding substrate rife with toxic allelochemicals (e.g. certain polyphenols) significantly retards larval development or in extreme cases, stops it. These authors analysed the larval development of Anastrepha ludens in 18 apple cultivars and compared it to an optimal host (i.e. Citrus paradisi or grapefruit), discovering that while the minimum time for larval development in grapefruit was 19 days (mean close to 37 days), in the case of the apple cultivar Schneiderapfel, the minimum larval developmental time was 54 days (mean close to 67 days)
Survival from larva to adult | Life history | Survival is one of the key elements of fitness (Brückner et al., 2018; Moretti et al., 2017). Only individuals that reach the adult stage have a chance to produce offspring. Host quality can have a strong effect on survival to adulthood. Birke and Aluja (2018) working with naturally growing native and exotic hosts reported that the mean adult emergence in A. ludens originating from white sapote (ancestral host) and criollo peach (exotic host) were 87% and 48%, respectively
Pupal weight | Morphology | Pupal weight is a morphological trait that is correlated with adult body size, which scales with many life-history traits that improve fitness (Brückner et al., 2018; Moretti et al., 2017). Starvation and desiccation resistance are positively correlated with body mass (Pascacio-Villafán et al., 2016). Larger males are more successful in defending a territory than smaller males and are more prone to gain matings (Aluja et al., 2008; Burk & Webb, 1983; Ekanayake et al., 2017). Lower body weight is associated with increased predation risk in males, and comes with reduced levels of energetic reserves, fertility and fecundity (Morimoto, Nguyen, et al., 2019; Newman et al., 2021). As is the case with length of larval development, pupal weight is strongly influenced by host quality. Aluja et al. (2014) reported mean pupal weights of 24 mg in A. ludens originating from grapefruit, whereas pupae from larvae developing in the apple cultivar Schneiderapfel (rife with polyphenols), weighted 10 mg on average. Birke and Aluja (2018) working with an ancestral host and several exotic hosts reported that the mean pupal weights of A. ludens originating from white sapote (ancestral host) and criollo peach (exotic host) were 23 and 11.5 mg, respectively
